title: PINN Design Stack & Feedback Loops
description: A ten-stage design architecture showing how upstream scientific choices constrain downstream realization and how validation evidence drives targeted redesign.
represents: The stack organizes a PINN study as four coupled phases rather than as neural-network training alone. It begins with the physical problem and computational role, translates these into representation and physics-enforcement choices, realizes them numerically, and closes the loop through reliability-oriented evaluation.
interpretation: The vertical 1→10 path is the dominant typical design sequence, not a universal recipe. Strong interdependence is shown only between specific stage choices that mutually constrain one another; phase rails are organizational labels rather than relationship arrows. Evaluation feedback returns the workflow to the earliest plausible design cause, and a redesign is accepted only after numerical, physical, robustness, uncertainty, and computational-cost checks improve.

phases.title: Problem Framing
phases.summary: Defines the scientific system, numerical demands, intended PINN role, and representation interface.

phases.title: PINN Formulation
phases.summary: Defines the trainable approximation and how governing knowledge and differential operators are realized.

phases.title: PINN Training
phases.summary: Defines where objectives are enforced, how losses are balanced, and how optimization is performed.

phases.title: PINN Reliability
phases.summary: Determines whether the resulting model is numerically accurate, physically faithful, robust, efficient, and reusable.

stages.title: Physical Problem Definition
stages.subtitle: Defines the physical system and its numerical demands
stages.summary: The governing structure, geometry, conditions, scales, regularity, and available data determine every downstream design choice.

evidence.rationale: The review frames physics-informed learning around governing laws, data, and computational task, supporting problem definition as the first design layer.
The canonical PINN paper formulates forward and inverse PDE problems from equations, conditions, observations, and unknown quantities.

stages.title: Physics Enforcement
stages.subtitle: Defines how governing knowledge constrains the model
stages.summary: Physics may enter through strong, weak, integral, hard, conservative, interface, or constitutive mechanisms with different admissibility and cost consequences.

evidence.rationale: The neural trial-solution construction satisfies boundary conditions by design, providing the historical basis for exact ansatz enforcement.
The paper compares boundary enforcement in PINNs and VPINNs and supports exact Dirichlet satisfaction as a distinct enforcement choice.
Conservative PINNs impose discrete conservation and interface flux continuity rather than relying on a pointwise PDE penalty alone.
VPINN accuracy depends on test functions and quadrature, showing that weak enforcement is a numerical formulation rather than a generic loss term.

stages.title: Evaluation and Validation
stages.subtitle: Determines reliability and guides redesign
stages.summary: Validation must combine solution error, residual diagnostics, physical fidelity, robustness, uncertainty, inverse recovery, computational cost, and benchmarks.

evidence.rationale: The review evaluates physics-informed learning across accuracy, physical consistency, data use, and computational roles rather than by training loss alone.

relationships.label: Problem definition frames the computational role
relationships.summary: Governing equations, domain, conditions, data, and regime define which computational task is scientifically meaningful.

relationships.label: Computational role specifies required inputs and outputs
relationships.summary: Forward, inverse, discovery, operator-learning, control, and uncertainty tasks require different model interfaces.

relationships.label: Input–output interface constrains representation choice
relationships.summary: State dimension, parameterization, geometry encoding, and requested outputs constrain the representation that can realize the task.

relationships.label: Representation must support the selected physics enforcement
relationships.summary: The approximation space must be compatible with the regularity, admissibility, and constraint mechanism used to impose the physics.

relationships.label: Physics formulation sets operator-evaluation requirements
relationships.summary: Strong, weak, integral, conservative, or hard enforcement determines which derivatives, quadrature rules, or discrete operators must be evaluated.

relationships.label: Residual realization informs constraint sampling
relationships.summary: The residual/operator implementation determines where evaluations are meaningful, affordable, and informative for collocation or quadrature.

relationships.label: Sampled constraints instantiate the composite objective
relationships.summary: Interior, boundary, initial, interface, data, or quadrature samples determine which objective terms are actually evaluated.

relationships.label: Objective structure conditions the optimization problem
relationships.summary: Loss scales, conflicts, curvature, and conditioning determine the numerical optimization problem presented to the training algorithm.

relationships.label: Training produces the candidate model to evaluate
relationships.summary: The trained state is not accepted until numerical, physical, robustness, uncertainty, and computational checks are performed.

relationships.label: Inputs / outputs ↔ representation
relationships.summary: The interface constrains architecture, while the representational strategy can require additional encoded inputs, latent variables, or auxiliary outputs.

evidence.rationale: Parameterized PINNs explicitly encode PDE parameters as latent inputs, demonstrating that representation design and the input-output interface must be chosen together.

relationships.label: Representation ↔ differentiation
relationships.summary: Representation regularity and basis choice affect usable derivatives, while derivative order and numerical differentiation cost constrain viable representations.

evidence.rationale: The reviewed methodology treats neural representation and differential-operator evaluation as coupled design choices because approximation regularity and derivative requirements jointly determine residual construction.
High-dimensional high-order differentiation cost motivates alternative residual evaluation, showing that derivative requirements feed back on practical representation design.

relationships.label: Physics enforcement ↔ differentiation
relationships.summary: The enforcement form determines derivative, quadrature, or discrete-operator requirements, while available operator evaluation can make one enforcement strategy preferable to another.

evidence.rationale: Variational residual evaluation makes test functions and quadrature explicit numerical choices, coupling weak enforcement directly to residual evaluation.
Coupled automatic and numerical differentiation changes residual realization and demonstrates that operator evaluation and enforcement cannot always be selected independently.

relationships.label: Physics enforcement ↔ loss construction
relationships.summary: Soft, hard, conservative, interface, and constitutive enforcement determine which loss terms exist, while loss formulation determines how softly enforced constraints compete during training.

evidence.rationale: Comparison of exact and penalty-based boundary enforcement shows that constraint mechanism changes whether boundary satisfaction appears as a competing loss term.
Conservative PINNs introduce conservation and interface-flux conditions that alter the objective structure relative to a pointwise PDE penalty alone.

relationships.label: Sampling ↔ loss construction
relationships.summary: Sampling determines which residuals contribute to the objective, while residual or loss information can be used to adapt the sampling distribution.

evidence.rationale: Loss-proportional importance sampling explicitly uses objective information to change collocation selection, demonstrating bidirectional sampling-loss dependence.
Residual-based adaptive refinement reallocates collocation points using current residual information, coupling objective diagnostics back to sampling.

relationships.label: Loss construction ↔ optimization
relationships.summary: Loss scaling, gradient conflict, curvature, and conditioning affect optimizer behavior, while optimization diagnostics motivate reweighting or reformulating the objective.

evidence.rationale: Gradient-flow analysis identifies stiffness and imbalance among composite PINN objectives and motivates gradient-informed balancing during optimization.
Loss-landscape analysis connects differential-operator conditioning to optimizer performance and motivates hybrid or curvature-aware optimization strategies.

relationships.label: Systematic model-form mismatch → revisit the physical problem

evidence.rationale: The reviewed evidence emphasizes matching physics-informed method and evaluation to the governing problem rather than assuming one universal formulation.

relationships.trigger: Systematic model-form, regime, or benchmark mismatch
relationships.action: Revisit governing assumptions, domain, conditions, forcing, or the target regime
relationships.message: Systematic model-form mismatch → revisit problem definition
relationships.summary: Only persistent evidence of a misframed physical problem should send the workflow back to Stage 1; ordinary training error should first be diagnosed downstream.

relationships.label: Task or repeated-query mismatch → reconsider the computational role

evidence.rationale: Repeated-query evaluation motivates moving from a single PINN solve to a learned solution operator.

relationships.trigger: The selected task is inefficient, ill-posed, or mismatched to repeated use
relationships.message: Task or repeated-query mismatch → reconsider computational role
relationships.summary: Evaluation can show that a single-solution PINN, inverse model, operator surrogate, or uncertainty formulation is the wrong computational role for the intended use.

relationships.label: Poor identifiability or missing state information → revise inputs / outputs

evidence.rationale: Explicit latent parameter encoding demonstrates how revising the input-output interface changes parameterized-PDE performance.

relationships.trigger: Poor identifiability, missing observables, or inadequate state coverage
relationships.action: Revise encoded inputs, auxiliary outputs, latent variables, or measured quantities
relationships.summary: Evaluation of inverse recovery or state reconstruction can reveal that the model interface does not expose the information needed by the task.

relationships.label: Spectral or localized approximation failure → change representation

evidence.rationale: Spectral failure of standard representations motivates Fourier-feature redesign for multi-scale PDEs.

relationships.trigger: Spectral bias, multiscale error, localized approximation failure, or inadequate capacity
relationships.action: Change architecture, basis, activation, decomposition, or network structure
relationships.message: Spectral / local approximation failure → change representation
relationships.summary: Persistent approximation structure in the validation error can identify representation rather than optimization as the dominant cause.

relationships.label: Constraint or conservation failure → reformulate physics enforcement

evidence.rationale: Conservation and interface-flux errors motivate a conservative discrete-domain reformulation.
Persistent boundary error motivates exact Dirichlet enforcement rather than penalty-only treatment.

relationships.trigger: Persistent boundary, interface, conservation, admissibility, or constitutive violation
relationships.action: Change strong/weak/integral formulation or soft/hard/conservative constraint mechanism
relationships.message: Constraint / conservation failure → reformulate physics enforcement
relationships.summary: Physical diagnostics can indicate that the governing constraints need a different enforcement mechanism rather than merely a larger penalty weight.

relationships.label: Derivative noise, memory, or operator cost → change residual evaluation

evidence.rationale: High-order derivative memory and runtime motivate trace-estimation reformulation.
Sparse or costly residual evaluation motivates coupled automatic–numerical differentiation.

relationships.trigger: Noisy/high-order derivatives, excessive memory, unstable residuals, or high operator cost
relationships.action: Reformulate derivative order, use auxiliary variables, numerical differentiation, or discrete residuals
relationships.message: Derivative / operator bottleneck → change residual evaluation
relationships.summary: Cost or instability traceable to derivative evaluation should redirect redesign to Stage 6 rather than to unrelated architecture or optimizer changes.

relationships.label: Localized error or poor coverage → adapt sampling

evidence.rationale: Residual-based adaptive refinement explicitly reallocates points from current residual information.

relationships.trigger: Localized error, under-resolved regions, weak boundary/interface coverage, or causal gaps
relationships.action: Resample collocation, boundary, interface, observation, quadrature, or time points
relationships.message: Localized error / poor coverage → adapt sampling
relationships.summary: Spatial, temporal, boundary, or interface error localization is a direct signal to reconsider where constraints are sampled.

relationships.label: Objective imbalance or competing constraints → rebalance the loss

evidence.rationale: Competitive loss progress is used to update adaptive objective weights during training.
Gradient statistics expose imbalance and drive learning-rate annealing across composite terms.

relationships.trigger: One objective dominates, gradients conflict, or constraints converge at incompatible rates
relationships.action: Rescale, reweight, normalize, or reformulate the composite objective
relationships.summary: Loss-term and gradient diagnostics should redirect redesign to objective construction when the failure is multi-objective imbalance rather than inadequate sampling.

relationships.label: Stagnation or unstable convergence → adjust training strategy

evidence.rationale: Ill-conditioned loss landscapes motivate hybrid and curvature-aware optimizer changes.

relationships.trigger: Optimization stagnation, unstable updates, slow convergence, or sensitivity to initialization
relationships.action: Change optimizer, learning rate, initialization, schedule, curriculum, staging, or stopping strategy
relationships.message: Stagnation / instability → adjust optimizer and training strategy
relationships.summary: When formulation and coverage are adequate but optimization fails to reach a useful solution, redesign should target Stage 9.
